question:
A 58-year-old woman presents to the physician with a throbbing headache. She says she had it for the last year and it’s usually located in the right temporal area. There is localized tenderness over the scalp. During the last 2 weeks, she experienced 3 episodes of transient loss of vision on the right side, without ocular pain. On physical examination, her vital signs are normal. Palpation reveals that the pulsations of the superficial temporal artery on the right side are reduced in amplitude. Laboratory studies show:
Blood hemoglobin 10.7 g/dL (6.64 mmol/L)
Leukocyte count 8,000/mm3 (8.0 x 109/L)
Platelet count 470,000/mm3 (470 x 109/L)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 60 mm/h (60 mm/h)
Which of the following conditions is most likely to co-exist with the presenting complaint in this woman?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "58-year-old woman with throbbing headache" -> "headache localized to right temporal area" -> "localized tenderness over the scalp" -> "reduced pulsations of superficial temporal artery" -> "transient loss of vision episodes" -> "elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate" -> "possible giant cell arteritis" -> "associated with polymyalgia rheumatica" -> 85%

CHAIN: "58-year-old woman with chronic headache" -> "temporal tenderness and reduced artery pulsation" -> "transient vision loss episodes" -> "high erythrocyte sedimentation rate" -> "suggestive of inflammatory condition" -> "polymyalgia rheumatica commonly coexists" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient presents with headache and vision loss" -> "temporal artery involvement indicated" -> "elevated inflammatory markers" -> "consideration of systemic inflammatory diseases" -> "polymyalgia rheumatica is a common association" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Throbbing headache and scalp tenderness" -> "reduced pulsation of temporal artery" -> "transient vision loss without pain" -> "high ESR indicates inflammation" -> "polymyalgia rheumatica often coexists with giant cell arteritis" -> 75%
analysis: The patient's symptoms, including a throbbing headache localized to the temporal area, scalp tenderness, and transient loss of vision, suggest a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis (GCA), which is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). The elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) further supports this inflammatory condition. PMR commonly coexists with GCA, especially in older adults. The other options, while they may have some association with headache or systemic symptoms, do not have the same strong correlation with the presentation of GCA as PMR does. Therefore, the most likely condition to coexist with the presenting complaint in this woman is polymyalgia rheumatica.
